children.value: You get one turn per round of combat, decided dynamically by your group and the initiative order, during which you can take any number of actions for which you have stamina.

A reaction in combat is a single action that you take outside of your turn. You can trigger your reaction at any time, including in the middle of another character’s turn; in such cases, your reaction is assumed to occur immediately after whichever action is being described, unless the spell or ability being used says otherwise. You can use your reaction either to
Expend 1 stamina to move up to half your movement distance, or
Expend 1 stamina to use one of your other available actions. Those action still cost their normal stamina amount, if they have a stamina cost.
The flexibility to invoke reactions is another reason to closely watch combat as it unfolds.
Here are a few cases to illustrate the use of reactions in combat:

An enemy pops out from behind a column to take a longbow shot at your companion. As the party’s ranged member, you call your reaction to shoot back at them. Once their attack is resolved, but before they move or attack again, you resolve your own attack on them.

Your team has set an ambush on an enemy troupe entering a cave. During the combat, your job is to shoot a rope holding up a cage at just the right moment. You watch during combat, and when the final enemy begins moving into region on the ground covered by the cage, you call your reaction shot. When that enemy finishes their movement, your slicing of the rope proceeds.

The “Arcane Redirection” spell specifies directly that it interrupts the process of another spell being cast. When used as a reaction, this spell details that a roll is made to attempt to redirect a spell being cast toward another target. Thus, if you call this reaction when another is describing some particular spell, it resolves before the spell effect as intended takes place. On the other hand, if your reaction was to cast a retaliatory attack spell against the caster, that would happen just after their own spell effect takes place.

This dynamic format for reactions is designed to allow for more engaging combat, but it can also be abused. Your GM has the final word on where a reaction slots in, and all players are encouraged to be respectful about taking reactions (particularly on another player’s turn). One system might be to raise a hand or token if you plan to take a reaction at the next available opportunity.
